newsitem.title: USA: Emerging market debt slips with U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market debt slips with U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: A dramatic selloff in the U.S. Treasury and stock markets sent emerging market debt prices lower, but emerging market debt experts said yield spreads widened only marginally.
"Brady prices have gone down but, at the same time, the spreads have actually widened only slightly," said one analyst.

Experts said emerging debt markets followed U.S. financial markets downward after U.S. economic data released earlier showed a strong first quarter retail sales scenario and a sharper-than-expected jump in March core producer prices.
The U.S. Labor Department reported earlier that the overall March PPI fell 0.1 percent while the core PPI, which excludes food and energy items, jumped 0.4 percent.

In addition, the U.S. Commerce Department reported a 0.2 percent rise in March retail sales, but also revised January and February sales upward to a gain of 1.5 percent and an advance of 1.7 percent respectively.
At 1630 EDT/2130 GMT, the U.S. Treasury 30-year bond was down 20/32 at 93.12 to yield 7.16 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off 148.36 to close at 6,391.69.
Trading sources noted that the fixed-rate instruments suffered bigger losses than the floating rate instruments because of the rising interest rate scenario.

At 1630 EDT/2130 GMT, Argentine pars were down one percentage point at 60-5/8 bid whereas its FRBs were off 3/4 at 88-1/2, and Mexican pars were down 3/4 at 69-3/4 whereas the country's discount bonds were off 1/2 at 86-3/8.
Emerging market experts said concerns that a strong March U.S. CPI report on Tuesday would prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates also hurt investor sentiment.

"People are still nervous about interest rates and stocks and until the picture gets clearer investors are not willing to put their cash to work," said one emerging market trader at a major U.S. investment bank.

"I think we will see more (downward) movement on the U.S. bond and as a result we will see more (downward) movement on the Brady market," said Walter Molano, director of financial and economic research at SBC Warburg in New York.
However, Molano added: "I think spreads will continue to widen out but just by a small amount."
As for the Ecuador eurobond issue scheduled for pricing next week, market experts said the timing is pretty bad.
"I think the timing right now is very poor for any kind of fixed income deal but especially for an exotic credit," said one market expert at a European bank.
"It will be awfully tough for the (Ecuadorean) government to get this off well given the interest rate environment right now," added James Barrineau, emerging market strategist at Smith Barney.
